data.content_ref: inline:The target's claim that the preference is 'not an inference about the future' contradicts the problem context's explicit statement that scientists choose theories 'to act on.' Action is inherently future-oriented; preferring a theory for action implies an expectation that it will continue to perform well or yield successful predictions. By framing corroboration merely as a structural necessity of the past ('only one left standing') while denying any inductive link to future utility, the target fails to explain the rationality of the *preference for action*. It dismisses the induction charge as a 'category mistake' without addressing why a Popperian agent should bet on the survivor if they cannot assume the future will resemble the past (the very principle of induction Popper rejected). The evolutionary analogy explains survival, not the rationality of betting on the survivor for future endeavors.
